description: We are a team of curious minds on a mission to make Mars more understandable and explorable. We combine science, technology, creativity, and collaboration to transform Martian data into an interactive map that helps future explorers find safe routes and discover fascinating places. We innovate today to explore new worlds tomorrow! 🚀
summary:
R.E.D. ATLAS is a survival map for a Marswalk on the floor of Melas Chasma, Valles Marineris. We fused real NASA orbital data (MRO CTX 20 m elevation models and 6 m mosaic, HiRISE, MOLA, HRSC+MOLA and THEMIS IR) into a 141,313-cell hexagonal terrain grid (about 5 m cells) with elevation, slope, sky visibility and radio line of sight to the base.

On that grid, a Rust engine plans the walk with a metabolic model of a suited astronaut, tracks how long the crew can safely stay out, and stress-tests the plan with 10,000 random multi-hazard simulations. In our scenario, a solar storm, a dust front, a radio shadow and soft ground hit at once. The base is 48 minutes away, beyond the 15-minute radiation window, so the engine re-plans in 17 ms and sends the astronaut to a rock shelter 9.4 minutes away. With automatic shelter switching, 96.0% of simulated missions stay safe, versus 23.8% when returning to base is the only option.

A habitat console (3D terrain, a three-layer "Spyglass" lens, route planner and EVA telemetry) turns this into one clear decision for the crew.
details:
What it does

R.E.D. ATLAS answers the question an astronaut and the habitat crew must answer during a Marswalk: "Can I still get back safely, and if not, where do I go?"

It covers one hyper-local route at 5 to 20 m resolution, the scale of a single spacewalk, where Mars Trek and global geologic maps stop being detailed enough. The route is a 4.9 km "Survival Triangle" in the southwest basin of Melas Chasma:

  • Base: an alluvial terrace.
  • WP1: hydrated sulfate deposits, a water resource (ISRU).
  • WP2: a steep, soft slope.
  • WP3: a rock alcove under an overhang used as a radiation shelter.

We moved the triangle 13.6 km from its first design after checking it against the real elevation model. At the original spot, the terrain showed neither the slope nor the cliff the scenario needed.

How it works

1. NASA data pipeline (Python). It searches the USGS Astrogeology STAC catalog and reads only the route window of each product: CTX DTMs at 20 m, HiRISE imagery, MOLA, HRSC+MOLA and THEMIS IR, plus the controlled CTX 6 m mosaic for the 3D texture. From these it derives slope, sky-view factor and line of sight to the base. Radio coverage uses single knife-edge diffraction for an S-band link. Everything is aggregated into H3 hexagons at resolution 9 (about 100 m) and 12 (about 5 m), stored as Parquet. A source manifest records every product used, its URL, licence and measured coverage.

2. Mission engine (Rust). It has five parts:

  • Terrain grid: loads the real grid with real H3 indices (h3o).
  • D* Lite planner: its cost is the metabolic power of a 170 kg suited astronaut on Mars. The model accounts for slope, regolith firmness and slip.
  • Walkback Limit Dual: at every moment it compares the time and radiation dose needed to reach the base or the shelter. When the base no longer fits within the flight rule (2 mSv per EVA), it switches the goal automatically.
  • Stochastic hazard engine (Markov/Poisson): runs the Chaos Mode Monte Carlo.
  • Deterministic safety state machine: five states, from nominal to shelter hold. It fuses simultaneous alarms into a single voice order shorter than 8 seconds, so the crew is not overloaded.

3. Base console (React, TypeScript, Three.js). It has four views:

  • 3D twin: the real terrain textured with CTX imagery, with switchable layers.
  • Spyglass lens: shows water, thermal inertia and relief under the cursor.
  • Route planner: shows the elevation, power and radio profile with a go/no-go verdict.
  • EVA telemetry: a timeline from T-45 to T+165 and the "return margin" bar. The astronaut can mark hazards and shelters during the walk, and the engine re-plans around them.

In our demo scenario (EVA-07), a solar particle event, a dust front, a radio shadow and soft regolith hit at the same time at T+105. The base is 48 minutes away over 2.15 km, beyond the 15-minute open-sky radiation window. The engine re-plans in 17 ms and sends the astronaut to the shelter, 9.4 minutes away over 595 m. In 10,000 Chaos Mode simulations, 96.0% of missions stay safe with automatic shelter switching, against 23.8% when the only option is returning to base.

Benefits

  • Every number has a provenance label: measured [M], derived [D] or scenario assumption [E]. The crew knows what is data and what is a design assumption.
  • The engine reproduces the reference timeline of the data pipeline within tight tolerances.
  • Decision figures are exported by the engine, not typed by hand.
  • The whole system runs offline on local data, as it would have to with a 3 to 22 minute delay to Earth.

What we hope to achieve

We want a reusable method to build a per-EVA survival map for any Mars site from open NASA data. Next steps:

  • run the Chaos Mode on the real grid instead of a synthetic corridor;
  • add a quantitative thermal-inertia layer and CRISM spectra;
  • run the engine on the suit computer with a local voice assistant, as described in our architecture document.

Tools and languages

  • Rust: h3o, parquet, serde.
  • Python: rasterio, rio-cogeo, pyproj, shapely, pyarrow, duckdb, h3, pystac-client, scipy, uv.
  • TypeScript: React, Vite, Three.js, Tailwind CSS.
  • Formats: Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF, GeoJSON, Apache Parquet.
  • Diagrams: Mermaid.
  • Testing: 263 Python tests and the Rust test suites.

What is design rather than implementation

These parts are specified in the architecture document but not built in this prototype:

  • the ROS 2 / Eclipse Zenoh link to the suit;
  • an on-suit language model and speech recognition;
  • the augmented-reality helmet display (its logic runs inside the console's EVA view).

Limitations

  • Thermal inertia values and the water content at WP1 are scenario assumptions [E]: no quantitative thermal-inertia map or CRISM product is available through the catalog for this site.
  • The shelter overhang cannot be seen in a 20 m elevation model.
  • The Chaos Mode currently runs on a synthetic corridor.
